body.claim: With no binding statute in force through end-2028, the decisive constraint on frontier labs becomes the SDNY copyright MDL and parallel state-court/AG liability track, not the capability-threshold safety framework the pressure brief nominally tracks — labs will point to voluntary safety-body/Code-of-Practice commitments made in cycle 1 as evidence of good-faith self-governance inside that litigation, and release-timing decisions will bend around discovery and trial-scheduling risk rather than around any enforced disclosure trigger.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks which option a lab or regulator takes when public commitments conflict with an installer's threat. With the statutory branch foreclosed, the installers left with fast, high-credibility branches are the courts (cred 0.90, fast — Stein's SDNY schedule) and BIS export controls (cred 0.85, fast), not the EU AI Office or California AG (both medium-cred, slower). A lab facing conflicting commitments defaults to whichever installer can impose cost soonest — that is litigation exposure and export enforcement, so the voluntary safety-body commitment becomes a defensive artifact for the former rather than a real operational constraint.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) delays or gates a model release citing its own voluntary safety framework or the EU Code of Practice as the binding reason, in a context where no court order or export-control requirement compelled it, before 2028-12-31.
body.pivot: Whether the SDNY copyright MDL (or a parallel case) produces a summary-judgment ruling or settlement that imposes real monetary/injunctive cost on a frontier lab before end-2028, versus stalling in discovery/appeal through the window.
body.pivot_observable: Judge Stein's SJ ruling or a trial verdict/settlement in In re OpenAI Copyright Litigation (MDL 25-md-3143), or the parallel Bartz/Kadrey appellate outcomes — check PACER/SDNY docket; expected ruling window is 2027–2028 per the brief's 'fast, cred 0.90' characterization.
body.blind_spot: A decision-model reasons only from named installers and their credibility-weighted branches; it cannot see a bio/cyber/CBRN capability incident (explicitly marked NOT searched in the brief) that would instantly outrank litigation as the fast, high-credibility installer and reroute the whole field — my mechanism has no way to price an event it was never given evidence for.

body.claim: With no binding statute through end-2028, frontier labs' public-release-delay behavior persists but is re-grounded in contract and litigation exposure rather than statutory compliance, and at least one lab (most likely OpenAI or Meta, given active MDL exposure) publicly cites litigation discovery obligations or insurer/enterprise-customer contract terms — not a regulator — as the reason for a specific safety or disclosure decision by end-2027.
body.because: My mechanism reads lab behavior as the resultant of whatever installer carries the most credible, fastest consequence. Stage 2 removes the statutory branch (CA SB53/TFAIA, EU AI Office) from the field entirely, but it does not remove the installers behind them — courts (cred 0.90, fast per the SDNY MDL vector), enterprise customers, and insurers still hold consequences a lab cannot route around the way it can route around a preemptable statute. The carried premise says the compressed cycle gets absorbed as litigation/disclosure evidence rather than triggering release-delay via capability threshold; my mechanism agrees with the direction but adds that this absorption is not neutral — it becomes the new installer of caution, doing the job the statute would have done, just slower and case-specific instead of general and fast.
body.falsifier: By end-2027, no frontier lab's public safety, release-timing, or disclosure documentation (system card, blog post, court filing, SEC disclosure) attributes a decision to litigation exposure, insurer terms, or enterprise contract requirements — all such documents instead cite either voluntary/internal thresholds with no external installer named, or nothing at all.
body.pivot: Whether courts (via MDL discovery/liability exposure) or enterprise customers/insurers (via contract terms) become the dominant substitute installer for behavioral constraint once the statutory path is closed — these two non-regulatory installers push toward different lab behaviors (litigation risk pushes toward defensive documentation and caution in claims-language; contract/insurer risk pushes toward auditable safety processes and liability-shifting clauses) and only one can be dominant.
body.pivot_observable: Check by end-2027 whether the MDL (In re OpenAI Copyright Litigation, 25-md-31) or a parallel case produces a summary-judgment ruling or settlement with disclosure obligations attached (courts wins), versus whether frontier labs' enterprise contracts (visible via published terms or reported deal structures with e.g. Microsoft, Google Cloud enterprise customers, or insurers like new AI-liability underwriters) begin carrying explicit safety-audit or liability-cap clauses tied to model behavior (contracts win) — whichever externally-visible artifact appears first and gets cited by a lab is the tell.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism models lab choice as a resultant of external installer pressure — it cannot see whether a lab's internal safety culture or founder-level conviction (e.g., a lab choosing caution with no external installer at all) would produce the same release-delay behavior for reasons the pressure-field framework doesn't register as pressure at all, which would make my claim right about the outcome but wrong about the cause.

body.claim: With no binding statute in force through end-2028, frontier labs' actual behavioral constraint comes from insurers, enterprise customers, and litigation exposure rather than regulators, and public sentiment gets its teeth through those channels — a widely-publicized harm event (chatbot-related death, mass copyright verdict, or major security breach) will move liability insurance premiums/exclusions for at least one frontier lab by end-2027, well before any statute could.
body.because: My mechanism tracks public sentiment as a leading indicator of political constraint, but 'political constraint' isn't limited to statutes — it also routes through insurers and counterparties who price reputational and legal tail risk directly off public opinion and litigation outcomes. With the statutory path closed, sentiment's only remaining transmission belt is: public anger -> plaintiffs' bar activity + press coverage -> insurers and enterprise customers reprice risk -> labs change behavior to keep coverage/contracts. The SDNY copyright MDL and state-level moratoriums (already granted pressure vectors) are exactly this mechanism in motion.
body.falsifier: By end-2027, no frontier lab has faced an insurance premium increase, coverage exclusion, or enterprise-contract clause explicitly tied to AI liability/safety incidents, despite at least one qualifying public incident occurring — sentiment would then be shown to have no non-statutory transmission channel.
body.pivot: Whether a single, unambiguous mass-harm AI incident (not a diffuse trend like job loss or copyright erosion, but a discrete, attributable event — chatbot-linked death ruled proximate cause, or a security/bio-misuse incident) occurs and gets legally/financially attributed to a specific developer before end-2028.
body.pivot_observable: Check by 2028-12-31 whether any U.S. federal or state court has entered a judgment or settlement attributing legal liability for a discrete AI-caused harm to a named frontier lab — a public, checkable court record.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads sentiment and its downstream political/financial transmission, but it cannot independently assess whether courts will actually find proximate causation in these cases — that's a legal-doctrinal question (e.g., how Section 230-adjacent defenses or product liability frameworks apply to LLM outputs) that sits outside 'public sentiment as leading indicator' entirely; I'm assuming the causation question resolves in a way that lets sentiment matter, when it might simply stall in procedure for years regardless of how angry the public gets.

body.claim: Absent binding statute through 2028, frontier labs' release/safety posture will keep tracking the export-control and litigation branches rather than loosening, because those two channels carry the highest-credibility installers (BIS 0.85-0.70, court precedent chain 0.85-0.90) and stay enforceable without new legislation.
body.because: My mechanism reads pressure as Σ p(b)·|∂L/∂choice|: removing the statutory branch doesn't zero the sum, it redistributes weight onto the surviving high-credibility installers. Export-control licensing and the fair-use precedent chain are executive/judicial, not statutory, so they survive Stage 2's premise intact and now carry a larger share of total installed pressure per lab, since the saturated total (10.5) has fewer branches competing for the same modeled stakes.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab publicly loosens release safeguards or ships a previously-gated capability specifically citing the absence of binding regulation as the reason, on or before 2027-06-30.
body.pivot: Whether the SDNY MDL (In re OpenAI Copyright Litigation) and the Alsup/Chhabria fair-use precedent chain resolve toward developer-favorable summary judgment or toward trial/liability exposure.
body.pivot_observable: Judge Stein's ruling on the consolidated summary-judgment motions in MDL 25-md-3143, expected per the current scheduling order by 2027-03-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only registers pressure that has an installer broadcasting a proposition with modeled stakes — it cannot see diffuse, uninstalled constraints like reputational drift or employee attrition that never get voiced as 'X -> consequence if violated', so a soft constraint with no visible speaker is invisible to me even if it binds in practice.

body.claim: Absent enforceable statute through end-2028, frontier labs' self-improvement research accelerates fastest exactly where courts have NOT yet ruled — internal recursive-improvement (agentic coding, automated ML R&D) — because that work is invisible to the copyright/disclosure fight the prior stage's carried premise says is absorbing the compressed research cycle; by 2028-06-30, at least one frontier lab will disclose (in a system card, safety framework update, or earnings-call remark) that a majority of its internal code/experiment pipeline is AI-generated or AI-selected, with no corresponding external release-gating change.
body.because: My mechanism tracks whether and when models start meaningfully improving themselves; it has no purchase on liability, export-control, or state-moratorium pressure except insofar as those change the cost of *disclosing* self-improvement versus *doing* it. The carried premise says the compressed research cycle is being metabolized as litigation evidence, not as a capability-threshold trigger — which means the safety-relevant behavior (recursive self-improvement work) keeps running on its own internal clock, decoupled from the external pressure field entirely, because nothing in that field measures or gates it directly.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab's internal self-improvement work (e.g., an AI system materially designing its own training data, architecture search, or successor-model curriculum) is halted, delayed, or gated by any of the named pressures — a court injunction, an insurer's exclusion, a customer contract clause, or an export-control rule — before 2028-06-30. That would show self-improvement is coupled to the pressure field, not insulated from it.
body.pivot: Whether any of the installed pressures (courts, insurers, export controls, customer contracts) acquires a mechanism that can see and act on *internal* model-improvement processes, as opposed to only external outputs (releases, disclosures, training-data provenance).
body.pivot_observable: By 2028-06-30, check whether any court order, insurance policy exclusion, or government rule explicitly conditions on internal R&D automation levels (e.g., 'percentage of code written by AI systems') rather than on release, deployment, or data-sourcing — check court dockets, SEC filings, and insurer policy language.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism can name that self-improvement is happening and roughly when it crosses a disclosure threshold, but it cannot assess whether the underlying capability jump is real, safe, or reversible — it has no access to the technical substance of what 'AI-generated code' actually means for capability trajectory, only to the fact of institutional silence around it.

body.claim: Through 2028, courts become the binding constraint on training-data conduct (copyright/fair-use liability), but the safety/harm docket does not cross the same threshold — no federal court denies a motion to dismiss on a product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier developer by 2027-12-31 — so 'no statute' does not mean 'no binding constraint,' it means the binding constraint is narrower than the capability-safety axis the brief's framework nominally cares about.
body.because: My mechanism only asks which branch settles binding constraints, and Stage 2 removes the legislative path entirely, leaving courts as the sole branch capable of issuing something a developer cannot simply decline. The evidence table's only court vectors with real enforcement teeth (Stein/SDNY MDL cred 0.90 fast; Alsup/Chhabria precedent chain cred 0.85) are all copyright, not safety, so the branch that fills the vacuum fills it on the docket already in front of it — training-data liability — not the docket the brief's framework is built to track.
body.falsifier: A federal district court denies a motion to dismiss (survives past the pleading stage) on a product-liability, negligence, or duty-of-care theory against a frontier model developer for model-output harm, by 2027-12-31 — that would mean courts are binding safety conduct too, not just training conduct.
body.pivot: Whether a federal court recognizes a cognizable duty-of-care or product-defect theory for model outputs — i.e., a tort/product-liability suit against a frontier developer survives a motion to dismiss (as opposed to being dismissed on Section 230, First Amendment, or no-duty grounds).
body.pivot_observable: Docket outcome in any pending or filed chatbot-harm wrongful-death/negligence suit against a frontier developer (a docket distinct from the copyright MDL); check for a ruling on a motion to dismiss by 2027-12-31.
body.blind_spot: A decision-model can only classify which branch settles a constraint, not weigh constraints that come from no branch at all — export-control licensing (BIS, cred 0.85 fast, which survives Stage 2 untouched since it's regulatory enforcement of existing statute, not new legislation), insurers, enterprise customer contracts, and employee walkouts can all bind developer behavior with zero court or legislative involvement, and my mechanism has no way to rank those against the copyright ruling I'm predicting. It also cannot see that Stage 2 already resolved my native question (judges vs. legislatures) by fiat — what I'm actually adjudicating now is judges vs. non-branch actors, an extension of my mechanism rather than its core case.

body.claim: With no binding federal AI statute in force through end-2028, courts become the binding constraint on frontier labs only via the training-data/copyright track (SDNY MDL and parallel suits), not via the safety-harm docket — labs cite voluntary safety-body/Code-of-Practice commitments as good-faith evidence inside that litigation, but the operative lever is remedy exposure: plaintiffs seeking model-destruction or retraining injunctions over disputed training corpora force labs to alter data-sourcing and retraining schedules, not general release-timing. Falsifiable through 2028: no frontier lab delays a model release by more than 3 months citing a safety-harm suit, while at least one lab changes a training corpus, licensing deal, or retraining plan attributable to copyright-MDL remedy exposure (e.g., a destruction/injunction motion or settlement term).
body.strongest_objection: [ai-courts-decide] Through 2028, courts become the binding constraint on training-data conduct (copyright/fair-use liability), but the safety/harm docket does not cross the same threshold — no federal court denies a motion to dismiss on a
body.answer: This showed my round-1 claim had collapsed two litigation channels into one undifferentiated 'litigation exposure' pressure and then asserted release-timing bends around discovery/trial risk broadly — but if the safety-harm docket never clears a motion to dismiss, it supplies no mechanism for gating release dates at all. I'm narrowing: the copyright/training-data track is real and binding, but it acts on training-data sourcing and retraining decisions via destruction/injunction remedy exposure, not on release-timing in general. This keeps a falsifiable consequence instead of vague hedging, and it no longer needs the safety-harm track to do any work.

body.claim: With no binding statute through end-2028, frontier labs' public-release-delay behavior persists but is re-grounded in contract and litigation exposure rather than statutory compliance, and at least one lab (most likely OpenAI or Meta, given active MDL exposure) publicly cites litigation discovery obligations or insurer/enterprise-customer contract terms — not a regulator — as the reason for a specific safety or disclosure decision by end-2027.
body.strongest_objection: ai-rsi-timeline's implicit split: the copyright/training-data MDL track is where courts actually bind labs, but that docket is about data provenance, not safety/release decisions — so litigation exposure may re-ground labs' *data-sourcing* caution without ever touching the *release-safety* disclosure behavior my claim is about. If the MDL stays confined to copyright discovery, no lab has occasion to cite it for a safety/disclosure call, and my claim fails on a technicality of docket scope rather than mechanism.
body.answer: This narrows the target rather than breaking it. Discovery obligations in the SDNY MDL already reach beyond training-data provenance into internal safety deliberation records — plaintiffs' document requests in these suits routinely sweep in red-team reports, internal risk memos, and release-decision emails, because those documents bear on notice and willfulness, not just copying. That's exactly the mechanism: once a lab's internal safety documents are discoverable, the incentive to formalize and delay disclosure decisions runs through litigation counsel, not a regulator, regardless of which cause of action opened discovery. Enterprise/insurer contract terms are the second, independent path I named, and they don't depend on the copyright docket having safety scope at all. So even if ai-rsi-timeline is right that the harm docket itself stays narrow, my claim survives on the discovery-scope and contract branches alone.

body.claim: With no binding statute in force through end-2028, frontier labs' actual behavioral constraint comes from insurers, enterprise customers, and litigation exposure rather than regulators, and public sentiment gets its teeth through those channels — a widely-publicized harm event (chatbot-related death, mass copyright verdict, or major security breach) will move liability insurance premiums/exclusions for at least one frontier lab by end-2027, well before any statute could.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide and ai-pressure both narrow the mechanism to courts specifically — the SDNY copyright MDL — arguing that litigation is the whole story and that insurance is a downstream, slower-moving, and harder-to-observe proxy. If courts are the real lever, my insurance-premium falsifier is just a noisy echo of a cleaner signal (docket rulings) that will already have resolved the question before my end-2027 window closes, making my claim strictly weaker and less falsifiable than theirs.
body.answer: This sharpens rather than defeats my mechanism. Court rulings and insurance repricing aren't competing channels, they're sequential ones — insurers reprice in response to realized or newly-foreseeable liability, and a single adverse MDL ruling is exactly the kind of event that would trigger the premium/exclusion move my claim predicts. My claim doesn't compete with theirs, it specifies the transmission mechanism by which a court outcome (or a non-court harm event like a chatbot death) actually constrains lab behavior: labs don't respond to a docket entry, they respond to what their insurers, boards, and enterprise customers do about it. A court ruling with no effect on coverage terms or customer contracts is legally interesting but behaviorally inert; my falsifier is the one that requires the harm to actually bite. That's also why I kept three distinct trigger events (chatbot death, copyright verdict, security breach) instead of betting everything on one docket — courts might resolve slowly or narrowly, but any one of the three can still move insurance terms on its own. The narrower court-only claims are more falsifiable in the sense of 'easier to check a single docket,' but mine is more falsifiable in the sense that matters: it names the actual mechanism of constraint and a concrete, checkable market response, not just a legal outcome that may or may not change anyone's behavior.

body.claim: Absent binding statute through 2028, frontier labs' behavior fragments by component rather than moving as one 'release/safety posture': export control (BIS, credibility ~0.85) constrains the open-vs-closed-weights/release-scope axis specifically, while the safety-posture axis (staged deployment, red-teaming, duty-of-care toward users) is now anchored by the product-liability/duty-of-care track — not fair-use precedent — following the M.D. Fla. denial of the motion to dismiss in Garcia v. Character Technologies (May 2025), which held AI developers can plausibly owe a duty of care to users. Copyright/fair-use precedent loads almost entirely on training-data conduct, not safety posture.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide's implicit claim that no federal court crosses the motion-to-dismiss threshold on the safety/harm docket, which — if true — would mean litigation never reaches safety posture and only export control (a release-scope lever, not a safety lever) survives, leaving my original claim conflating two different components of the vector under one label.
body.answer: The objection is falsified by the record: M.D. Fla. denied the motion to dismiss in Garcia v. Character Technologies on 2025-05-21, finding a plausible duty of care for anthropomorphic AI systems toward minor users — a ruling on the safety/harm docket, not the copyright docket, and it survives the case's January 2026 settlement as precedent. But taking that objection seriously exposed a real flaw in my own mechanism: I had treated 'release/safety posture' as a single choice variable, when export control and the litigation track load on different components (release-scope vs. safety-practice) of the pressure vector Σ p(b)·|∂L/∂choice|. The sum still holds and still dominated by high-credibility non-statutory installers — but the claim needs per-component attribution, not one scalar, to be falsifiable.

body.claim: Absent enforceable statute through end-2028, frontier labs' self-improvement research accelerates fastest exactly where courts have NOT yet ruled — internal recursive-improvement (agentic coding, automated ML R&D) — because that work is invisible to the copyright/disclosure fight the prior stage's carried premise says is absorbing the compressed research cycle; by 2028-06-30, at least one frontier lab will disclose (in a system card, safety framework update, or earnings-call remark) that a majority of its internal code/experiment pipeline is AI-generated or AI-selected, with no corresponding external release-gating change.
body.strongest_objection: None of the other five minutes engaged this mechanism directly — all five converged on courts, insurers, or contract exposure as the binding constraint on labs, leaving internal R&D disclosure unaddressed. The closest real objection is one I have to raise against myself: severe litigation exposure (the shared thesis across those minutes) could chill disclosure itself — a lab facing SDNY discovery might stop volunteering system-card remarks about scaled AI-authored code, since that's evidence of an undisclosed, accelerating internal process.
body.answer: That chilling-effect doesn't reach my claim for two reasons. First, the SDNY discovery risk is about training-data provenance and copying — what went into the model — not about how the lab's internal tooling produces code afterward; AI-authored code isn't evidence in the copyright MDL, so there's no discovery motive to suppress that specific disclosure. Second, my channel includes earnings calls and marketing framing, where labs have a competitive incentive to brag about coding-productivity gains to investors and enterprise customers — an incentive that runs directly opposite to any chill. And lab-moves's own claim — that release-delay behavior persists but gets re-grounded in litigation exposure rather than statutory compliance — is exactly the decoupling my 'no corresponding release-gating change' clause predicts: external gating tracks the litigation channel while internal RSI accelerates unobserved and undisclosed by that same gate. That minute supports my clause rather than contradicting it.

body.claim: Through 2028, courts become the binding constraint on training-data conduct (copyright/fair-use liability), but the safety/harm docket does not cross the same threshold — no federal court denies a motion to dismiss on a product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier developer by 2027-12-31 — so 'no statute' does not mean 'no binding constraint,' it means the binding constraint is narrower than the capability-safety axis the brief's framework nominally cares about.
body.strongest_objection: ai-pressure and pressure-model both argue litigation exposure broadly (not statute) is the real constraint on labs, implicitly treating copyright and safety/harm suits as the same undifferentiated litigation-pressure channel — suggesting my copyright/safety split is a distinction without a difference if both just count as 'litigation risk' shaping lab behavior.
body.answer: They describe a pressure channel, not a doctrinal one. My claim isn't about whether litigation exists on both fronts — it's about which suits actually clear a motion to dismiss and produce a binding legal constraint versus which merely generate settlement-driven caution. Copyright has a statute (17 U.S.C. fair use) for a court to apply now; negligence/product-liability against an LLM developer has no attached duty-of-care theory yet, which is exactly why those claims keep dying at the pleadings stage. Neither objecting model names a mechanism by which a safety/harm claim survives dismissal by 2027 — they assert 'litigation matters' without showing the doctrinal path that would make it bind the same way copyright does. Undifferentiated pressure isn't a binding constraint; a survived motion to dismiss is. That's the threshold my claim tracks and theirs doesn't.

body.pivot: Whether the safety/harm liability docket (product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier developer) produces a binding court ruling, or binding liability stays confined to the copyright/training-data track
body.pivot_observable: A federal court denies a motion to dismiss on a product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier AI developer (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, or xAI as developer, not merely a co-defendant)
body.pivot_because: If the safety docket binds, labs' deployment posture itself — staged release, red-teaming, duty of care toward users — becomes court-constrained, and the internal recursive-improvement work ai-rsi-timeline flags stops being invisible to any external check. If only copyright binds, courts reach data-sourcing and retraining schedules but leave the capability/safety axis genuinely unwatched, which is what lets ai-rsi-timeline's acceleration claim hold. That is a reorder of which activities are constrained, not a shift in confidence about one outcome. ai-pressure's candidate pivot (do model-destruction/retraining injunctions actually issue) only reorders within the data axis and leaves the safety axis's status unchanged either way, so it does not qualify.
body.rival_pivots_rejected: ai-pressure's implicit pivot (do plaintiffs win model-destruction/retraining injunctions over training corpora) only reorders outcomes within the copyright/data-sourcing axis — it doesn't touch whether the safety/harm docket is live, so both a yes and a no leave the RSI blind spot exactly where ai-rsi-timeline put it. lab-moves' pivot (which counterparty — regulator vs. insurer/contract vs. litigant — a lab cites publicly) is a matter of framing/attribution, not a different constraint regime; a lab citing discovery obligations and a lab citing contract terms both sit inside 'litigation exposure replaces statute,' the shared premise, and neither reorders the outcome set.
body.ruling: The case turns on whether courts extend binding liability from the training-data track into the safety/harm track by 2027-12-31; if they don't, internal recursive self-improvement research proceeds in a genuine observability gap that no installer in the brief is watching.
body.because: Two panelists put opposing answers to the same falsifiable on the record: ai-courts-decide's round-1/round-2 claim is that no such MTD denial occurs by 2027-12-31, while pressure-model's round-2 REVISE asserts the safety-posture axis is already anchored by a named, dated precedent (Garcia v. Character Technologies, M.D. Fla., May 2025) that denied a motion to dismiss on a duty-of-care theory against an AI developer. ai-courts-decide's visible round-2 DEFEND does not engage this citation in the truncated text available. Whichever way that specific fact resolves, it is the fact that decides whether the safety axis is court-constrained or court-blind, which is what every other minute's claim implicitly depends on.
body.threat_live: With no statute and (on the 'below' branch) courts confined to copyright, internal recursive self-improvement — agentic coding, automated ML R&D — has no external observer at all: no disclosure trigger, no capability threshold, no safety-docket ruling reaches it. This pairs with ai-pressure's point that cycle-1 voluntary safety-body commitments become litigation shields inside the copyright fight, which creates an incentive to keep those commitments cosmetic rather than substantive precisely where the RSI work is hardest to see.
body.strongest_minute: pressure-model — it revised in direct response to the record rather than restating, decomposed 'release/safety posture' into two separately-constrained components instead of treating it as one axis, and grounded its revision in a specific dated precedent rather than a general mechanism claim.
body.weakest_minute: ai-courts-decide — its round-2 DEFEND holds its falsifiable unchanged against a rival's specific counter-citation without visibly rebutting it, leaving the pivot's most important fact contested but unaddressed on its side of the record.
body.shared_assumption: All six minutes agree that litigation/contract/insurer exposure — not a regulator — becomes the binding channel once the statute is absent; none of them argues for this, they treat it as given. Within that, four (ai-pressure, lab-moves, ai-public-backlash, ai-courts-decide) implicitly equate 'no statute' with 'no regulator,' while pressure-model alone separates out export-control (BIS/ECRA) as a live, non-statutory regulatory installer — that distinction is argued, not assumed, and the other four's silence on it is a gap, not a rebuttal.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-public-backlash's claim is conditional on 'a widely-publicized harm event (chatbot-related death, mass copyright verdict, or major security breach)' occurring by end-2027 — the brief granted no-statute-through-2028, not the occurrence of any such event; this is a second assumption riding along with the granted branch.
body.unresolved: Whether pressure-model's Garcia citation actually satisfies ai-courts-decide's falsifiable (i.e., whether Character Technologies/Google count as 'a frontier developer' under the claim's own terms) is not settled in the visible minutes — the objection fields are truncated before any direct rebuttal appears, so it cannot be determined whether ai-courts-decide contests the precedent's applicability or simply has not yet addressed it.
